Case study · Agentic software delivery · Part 2

Federating IMDb: an agentic build at three speeds

211 million documents behind one federated GraphQL endpoint; a poster-rich browsing UI whose chatbot inherits exactly your permissions; and enterprise-grade field-level governance run from its own control plane — built by AI agents working at three deliberately different levels of formality, from vibe coding to the full ticket-driven SDLC of part one.

Daniel Perez · July 2026 · github.com/dperez4787

211Mdocuments federated
8 + 1Java subgraphs + Cosmo router
6repositories, one system
~130mswarm p50 through the router

Goals

Functional

  1. An extremely snappy, rich IMDb data experience — every public IMDb dataset available through one UI: titles, people, ratings, episodes, crews, regional titles, and the 100-million-row principals collection.
  2. Sort by popularity, everywhere — titles rank by vote counts for free; people needed a materialized popularity score computed from the work they're known for.
  3. Search facets — vocabulary dropdowns (every genre, every credit category) and live counts that narrow with the filter: “Drama (5,646)”.
  4. Images for titles — poster art in the browsing experience, not just rows of text.
  5. Enterprise-grade, field-level governance and security — individual fields like Rating.numVotes or Name.birthYear grantable per role, administered from a control-plane UI, enforced live with no redeploys.

Technical

  1. Use AI to build the application — at varying degrees of formality. One system, three delivery styles: full ticket-driven rigor, lightweight file-based tickets, and pure vibe coding. Measure what each buys.
  2. A proof-of-concept of open-source GraphQL federation — WunderGraph Cosmo composing eight Netflix DGS subgraphs, with custom Go router modules instead of a commercial control plane.

The product

Marquee: the browsing experience the graph was shaped for

Marquee is the face of the system — a React SPA on Firebase Hosting at dfp-imdb-browser.web.app, Google-sign-in gated, that consumes only the federated endpoint. No REST side doors, no direct database reads: every poster grid, facet count, and cast list is a GraphQL operation against the router, authenticated with the signed-in user's own Firebase ID token. It was built by a five-agent team (a product owner, a UI/UX designer, an architect, a developer, and a tester) working from markdown tickets checked into the repo itself — more on that in the formality section below.

Browse & search — popularity-ranked, faceted, poster-rich · the snappy part

The home screen is one search box with keystroke-speed autocomplete across titles and people. “Browse all titles” opens the faceted view: genre, type, year, rating, and people filters with live counts that narrow as you stack them (“Drama · 5,646”), default-sorted by the materialized popularity score, every result carrying poster art. Counts over 10,000 are honestly capped (“10,000+ titles”), and the header states when the search index was last rebuilt — a freshness signal the orchestrator exposes as searchInfo.rebuiltAt.

Title & person pages — governance you can see · restricted fields render as locks, not lies

Detail pages cross-navigate the whole graph: a title's directors, writers, and cast link to people; a person's known-for mosaic and filmography link back to titles. The interesting part is what happens when the graph withholds a field. Marquee never fakes a value and never hides that something exists: a governed field the current role hasn't been granted renders as a lock chip — “Vote count is governed data this app hasn't been granted. If access is granted, it appears here automatically.” The header badge shows who the graph thinks you are (here: no data role), so the UI's honesty is traceable to a persona.

Concierge — a chatbot with exactly your permissions · GraphQL MCP against the live router

Concierge is the “ask anything about the data” panel. It is not a canned FAQ: a server-side agentic loop (Claude, streaming over server-sent events) is handed two MCP tools — introspect-schema and query-graphql — from mcp-graphql, an open-source GraphQL MCP server spawned per request and pointed at the router's /graphql. The model reads the live schema, writes real operations, and answers from what comes back.

The security property that makes this safe is one line of configuration: the MCP server forwards the requesting user's own Firebase ID token as its Authorization header. The bot has no service credential and no super-user view — its data access is exactly the signed-in user's, so field-level governance applies to the chatbot for free. Ask it for a birthday and, if your role can't read Name.birthYear, the graph withholds the field and Concierge says so — explicitly instructed to never guess a governed value — with the restricted coordinate surfaced right in the chat. Guardrails are deliberately boring: eight tool-iterations max, capped response tokens, per-user rate limiting, and a system prompt that pins answers to the graph.

The full setup is documented in the repo: the chat-backend contract in docs/architecture.md, the service itself in app/chat, and the tickets that specified it (IMDB-10, IMDB-11, IMDB-16).

Architecture

One router, eight subgraphs, two UIs

The centerpiece is imdb-federation — a single Maven mono-repo holding all eight Java subgraphs as modules: one shared Dockerfile parameterized by module, one paths-filter matrix that builds only what changed, one common/ library, eight Cloud Run services out the other end. The mono-repo is what made “stamp out seven more subgraphs from the proven pattern” a one-day exercise instead of seven repo setups. Every box below is a link — the subgraphs go straight to their module directories.

The data

Two hundred eleven million documents, honestly imported

Everything sits on 211 million MongoDB documents — seven IMDb TSV files that a Cloud Run Job re-imports every Sunday at 06:00 UTC. The pipeline is a Node orchestrator that spawns mongoimport per file and is fussy about exactly the things that matter at this scale:

  • Streaming, never buffering. Each file is downloaded, gunzipped, and cleaned in one pipe: IMDb's \N null sentinels are blanked in-stream and dropped by --ignoreBlanks, so missing values are simply absent — idiomatic Mongo, and free “sorts last” behavior downstream. Memory stays flat no matter the file size.
  • Typed at the door. --columnsHaveTypes with an explicit field spec per file makes averageRating a double and startYear an int32 at import time — queryable and indexable without a reshaping pass over 100M rows. A stray unparseable value drops that one field, not the run.
  • Atomic promotes. Every file imports into <collection>_staging, indexes build there, then a single renameCollection with dropTarget swaps it over the live name. Readers never see an empty, partial, or unindexed collection, and a failed run never touches live data — retries are idempotent by construction.
  • Sequential, biggest last. The M-tier cluster is the write bottleneck, not the container, so files import one at a time with the 100M-row principals file last.
CollectionRowsKey indexes
title_principals100.4M{tconst, ordering} unique · {nconst} for “everything this person touched”
title_akas58.4M{titleId, ordering} unique
name_basics15.5M{nconst} unique
title_basics12.6M{tconst} unique
title_crew12.6M{tconst} unique
title_episode9.8M{tconst} unique · {parentTconst} for season listings
title_ratings1.7M{tconst} unique

The Atlas instance is an M20 in GCP us-central1 — deliberately the same region as every Cloud Run service, so import and query traffic never leaves the region. Numbers from the first full import: 33.8 GB of logical data compresses to 10.1 GB on disk, plus 12.2 GB of indexes, on a 36 GB volume with auto-scaling on (the staging copy of whichever collection is importing needs the headroom — for principals, that peak matters). The full 211M-row import takes about 1h50m on the M20; on the original M10 it projected at 5–7 hours, a tidy demonstration that the cluster, not the container, is the bottleneck. One operational scar worth repeating: never overlap an import with an Atlas topology change — a rolling resize interrupts index builds while the import's write load stalls the resize, and they starve each other.

On top of the source collections, the orchestrator subgraph maintains two derived collections it rebuilds on demand — search_titles and search_names — with genres split into real arrays, ratings merged in, and a materialized popularity for people: explode 45M known-for credits into a temp collection, join the 1.7M rated titles, and sum vote counts per person. Bryan Cranston outranks a prolific-but-obscure character actor, exactly as a search box should behave, and the sort is a plain descending index.

The build

Two entities, eight owners of the truth

The federation design fell out of the data. Two things in this world have identity — a title (tconst) and a person (nconst) — so the graph has exactly two entities. Each collection became a subgraph that either owns an entity (titles, names) or contributes fields to it (ratings, episodes, crew, akas, principals), and the eighth — the orchestrator — owns search. The load-bearing trick is the key stub: when the crew subgraph says “directed by nm0005690,” it returns a Name stub marked resolvable: false, and the router hydrates the person from the names subgraph in a parallel _entities hop. No subgraph ever reads another subgraph's collection.

The riskiest assumption was proven first: that a DGS entity fetcher could batch through a DataLoader so N representations collapse into one indexed $in query rather than N+1 lookups against a 100M-row collection. The keystone subgraph shipped with a Mongo CommandListener that counts every command the driver sends — assertThat(counter.count("find")).isEqualTo(1) — and that batching-proof assertion became house style across all 114 tests. With the keystone green, the remaining subgraphs were stamped from the same pattern and went green on the first full run.

Search earns its own collections

“Top-rated Sci-Fi from the 70s and 80s” is not a query the source collections can answer: genres are comma-joined strings, ratings live apart from years, and the import pipeline atomically replaces any collection you dare to index. Hence the derived collections above. Facets come in two typed flavors — materialized vocabularies and contextual $facet counts capped at the same 10k budget as totals — because the tempting alternative, a GraphQL field that accepts a raw aggregation pipeline, is an injection surface, an unbounded-cost surface, and a schema-contract vacuum. The API reports what it approximated (titleCandidatesCapped) instead of pretending exactness over 12.6M rows.

The honest ledger: what the fast path cost

Marquee's keystroke-speed search is anchored token/prefix matching against the derived collections — a deliberate trade away from Mongo's $text search, which couldn't hit the latency budget (the conformance work is ticketed as IMDB-18). “Faster but less advanced” deserves a precise answer, and most of what was dropped was ranking machinery working against this use case. Still, three regressions are real:

  • Stemming is gone. $text stemmed English words, so “godfathers” found The Godfather. Now a single word matches exactly, and only the last word of a multi-word query prefix-matches. Modest impact for title and name search — people mostly type the actual words — but it's real.
  • Diacritic folding is gone. $text matched “amelie” → Amélie; token equality won't. This is the one users are most likely to notice on an international catalog. The fixes are known if it stings: fold diacritics at rebuild time and query time (expressible, just ugly), or Atlas Search down the road.
  • Misspellings return empty instead of something. “Bety la fea” used to return results — but look at what they were: fifteen seconds of every title containing “la”. Neither the old nor the new search does fuzzy matching; the old version just disguised misses as noise. Empty-in-200ms is arguably the better failure, but it looks stricter to users.

The router is the only door

Auth splits into two boundaries with two token types, and the subgraphs needed zero auth code for either. Client → router: stock Cosmo JWT verification against Google's JWKS — anonymous requests die with 401 before any GraphQL work. Router → subgraphs: Cloud Run IAM. The subgraphs deploy with --no-allow-unauthenticated, and the router's subgraphtoken module mints a Google-signed ID token per subgraph audience; a direct call to any subgraph gets 403 from Google's front end before Spring Boot ever sees it. That perimeter is what makes single-point field enforcement honest.

The governance plane

Declare at the edge, decide at the center, enforce at the gate

Field-level governance follows one rule — each layer does exactly one job, and no job is done twice:

  • Subgraphs declare. A custom DGS directive marks sensitive fields in the schema, next to the code that owns the data: numVotes: Int! @governed(reason: "vote counts are analyst-only"). At startup each subgraph registers its declarations with the policy service. It never evaluates authorization at runtime.
  • The policy service decides. imdb-policy-service is the system of record — a Spring Boot + MongoDB service holding governed fields, role policies, personas, and an append-only audit log in its own imdb_governance database. It publishes a versioned, ETag-cached policy bundle, maps signed-in Google identities to personas, mints playground tokens, and serves the control-plane UI you see below from the same Cloud Run service. Like the federation itself, it was vibe-coded — the governance plane took shape in conversational sessions, not tickets.
  • The router enforces. The fieldauth Go module polls the bundle (~15 seconds, fail-static on outage), resolves every selected field of an operation to a schema coordinate — aliases, fragments, union spreads included — and withholds the coordinates the caller's roles can't read, annotating the response with extensions.governance: the redacted field list, the deciding bundle revision, and the caller's roles. That annotation is what lets Marquee render truthful lock chips and Concierge explain a denial instead of hallucinating around it.
The control plane, read-only · what anyone can see

The UI's read views come straight from the public bundle: every governed coordinate with its allowed roles, each subgraph's @governed declarations exactly as registered at startup, and the live federated schema introspected from the router at runtime — governed fields highlighted, everything else open by posture (allow-unless-governed; a governed field with no roles denies everyone). Admin operations sit behind a token.

Same query, two personas · the playground against the real router

The playground mints a token for each persona and runs the same operation against the production router, side by side. As public: Game of Thrones' average rating comes back but the vote count is withheld, and extensions.governance names Rating.numVotes as redacted, decided by bundle revision 8. As analyst: numVotes: 2632698. Flip a grant and rerun — the outcome changes within one poll interval, no deploy.

Admin: grants, personas, audit · with the admin token set

With the admin token, the same views become the write surface. Each governed coordinate carries its declaration reason and registration timestamp, and roles are granted or revoked inline — Save bumps the bundle revision and the router picks it up within a poll. Personas map Google emails to roles (a user mapped nowhere has no roles and sees only ungoverned fields — that's the “no data role” badge in Marquee's header). And every change lands in the append-only audit trail: the revision history reads like a story — seeds, subgraph registrations, the live demo's grant-and-revert on Rating.numVotes, an admin deleting policies back to deny-everyone.

Verified live

Against production: an analyst reads Rating.numVotes (2.6M votes for Game of Thrones); public gets the same query answered with the field withheld and named in extensions.governance; an admin grant flipped the outcome live within one 15-second poll — bundle revision bump, no deploy — and the revert re-denied. The audit trail records every step.

The experiment

Three speeds of formality

The technical goal worth the most was not the federation — it was watching the same developer-agent capability deliver under three different process regimes, and seeing what each one costs and buys.

RepositoryMethodologyHow it ran
linear-exampleformalLinear tickets with acceptance criteria as the spec; remote agents claim tickets from a board; draft-PR gate; tester verdicts; human merges — part one
imdb-browsersemi-formal18 markdown tickets checked into the repo's own tickets/ directory; five agents (product-owner, ui-ux-designer, architect, developer, tester); one PR per ticket
imdb-federationvibe-codedConversational sessions; keystone-first strategy; rigor supplied by the batching-proof test convention, not process
cosmo-routervibe-codedConversational sessions; custom Go modules de-risked by a spike, verified by smoke tests against the live deploy
imdb-policy-servicevibe-codedConversational sessions from a written plan; 15 integration tests before first deploy
imdb-data-pipelinevibe-codedConversational sessions; correctness carried by unit tests and the staging-rename design rather than tickets
Speed 1 · Vibe codingThe platform: federation, router, policy service, pipelinefastest

The platform layers — eight subgraphs, the custom router, two auth boundaries, the governance plane, the import pipeline — were built by vibe coding: conversational sessions with Claude Code, no tickets, no formal acceptance criteria. It was by far the fastest mode. What kept it honest was engineering convention in place of process: prove the riskiest assumption first, and make every claim falsifiable in a test.

Speed 2 · File-based ticketsMarquee (imdb-browser)the optimization

The product ran one notch more formal: markdown tickets versioned in the repo itself — intentionally in git, not Linear. Each ticket carries acceptance criteria, a dependency list, a branch name, and the PR that closed it, so the process history lives beside the code it produced. The full catalog is below; tickets kept a five-agent team honest without a board, a poller, or any ceremony beyond the repo.

Speed 3 · The full agentic SDLClinear-examplethe rigor

At the formal end sits part one: a product owner, architect, developer, and tester coordinating through Linear, remote agents claiming tickets from a board, draft-PR gates the platform enforces, and a human whose only actions are two status changes and a merge click.

The point of the spectrum is that formality scales to the stakes — and to the author. Vibe coding was the right speed for an expert-steered infrastructure build where the operator could supply judgment interactively. File tickets were right for a product with clear scope and a fast feedback loop. And the fully formal end is not bureaucracy for its own sake: when acceptance criteria on a ticket are the specification, and implementation and verification run remotely against that specification, the person driving delivery no longer has to be an engineer. That is the trajectory part one states explicitly: dial the formality up and the same pipeline lets product owners and designers drive their own application development — engineering rigor supplied by the process, not gated on engineering availability.

Where it stands

Live, governed, and one endpoint wide

Eight subgraphs, the router, the policy service, the chat backend, and Marquee are live on Cloud Run and Firebase Hosting behind two auth boundaries. The full dataset is imported weekly, searchable, faceted, poster-rich, and governed at the field level from a control plane whose every decision is audited. The chatbot answers from the same graph with the same permissions as the person asking. Try it yourself: Marquee is open to anyone with a Google account at dfp-imdb-browser.web.app.

Both posts in this series are built and shipped the same way their subjects were — this one arrived through the pipeline described in part one, which also records what every feature cost to the cent.
